The values differ, but they are centered near the population proportion.

title: 9  Sampling Distributions
text:
9.5 What Is a Sampling Distribution?
A sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic calculated from all possible random samples of the same size from a population.
To imagine one:

Draw a random sample of size \(n\).
Calculate a statistic, such as \(\hat{p}\) or \(\bar{x}\).
Return to the population and draw another random sample of the same size.
Calculate the statistic again.
Repeat the process many times.
Plot all the resulting statistics.

The resulting graph is not a distribution of individual people or cases. It is a distribution of sample statistics.






WarningThree distributions can be confused




A population distribution contains individual values for the entire population.
A sample distribution contains individual values in one sample.
A sampling distribution contains statistics calculated from many samples.

title: 9  Sampling Distributions
section: 9.6 The Center of a Sampling Distribution
text:
9.6 The Center of a Sampling Distribution
The sampling distribution of a sample proportion is centered at the population proportion:
\[
\mu_{\hat{p}}=\pi
\]
Similarly, the sampling distribution of a sample mean is centered at the population mean:
\[
\mu_{\bar{x}}=\mu
\]
An individual sample may overestimate or underestimate the population value. Across many random samples, however, the statistics balance around the parameter. This is why random sampling can provide useful estimates.

title: 9  Sampling Distributions
text:
9.7 The Spread: Standard Error
A sampling distribution also has variation. Its standard deviation is called the standard error.
For a sample proportion:
\[
SE_{\hat{p}}=\sqrt{\frac{\pi(1-\pi)}{n}}
\]
where:


\(\pi\) is the population proportion; and

\(n\) is the number of cases in each sample.

The standard error describes the typical amount of chance variation in sample proportions. A smaller standard error indicates that estimates tend to cluster more closely around the population parameter.






WarningSample size is not the number of repeated samples



In the formula, \(n\) is the number of cases within each sample. It is not the number of samples used to imagine or simulate the sampling distribution.

title: 9  Sampling Distributions
text:
9.8 Sample Size and Precision
Suppose \(\pi=0.40\). The standard error changes as the sample size increases:


Sample size
Standard error



\(n=10\)
\(\sqrt{0.40(0.60)/10}=0.1549\)


\(n=25\)
\(\sqrt{0.40(0.60)/25}=0.0980\)


\(n=100\)
\(\sqrt{0.40(0.60)/100}=0.0490\)



Larger samples have smaller standard errors. Their sample proportions tend to fall closer to the population proportion.







Figure 9.1: As sample size increases, the sampling distribution becomes narrower while remaining centered at the population proportion.










NotePrecision is not the same as accuracy



A larger random sample reduces chance variation. It does not correct biased selection, poor measurement, missing cases, or other systematic problems.

title: 9  Sampling Distributions
text:
9.9 Why Sampling Distributions Become Normal
Under appropriate conditions, sampling distributions are approximately normal. This result is connected to the central limit theorem.
For sample means, the sampling distribution becomes increasingly normal as sample size grows, even when the population itself is not perfectly normal. For sample proportions, the approximation works when the expected numbers of cases in both categories are sufficiently large.
The important practical lesson is that a sample statistic can often be evaluated using the normal curve. We can locate it with a z-score and determine whether it is common or unusual under an assumed population value.

title: 9  Sampling Distributions
section: 9.10 A z-Score for a Sample Proportion
text:
9.10 A z-Score for a Sample Proportion
In Chapter 8, a z-score measured the distance of an individual value from a mean in standard deviation units. For a sample proportion, we use the same logic but divide by the standard error:
\[
z=\frac{\hat{p}-\pi}{SE_{\hat{p}}}
\]
The score tells us how many standard errors the sample proportion falls above or below the population proportion.

title: 9  Sampling Distributions
text:
9.11 Worked Example: Property-Crime Proportions
Suppose the population proportion of property crimes in Smashitburg is \(\pi=0.30\). A random sample of 150 incidents produces \(\hat{p}=0.41\).

9.11.1 Step 1: Calculate the Standard Error
\[
SE_{\hat{p}}
=\sqrt{\frac{0.30(1-0.30)}{150}}
=\sqrt{0.0014}
=0.0374
\]

9.11.2 Step 2: Calculate the z-Score
\[
z=\frac{0.41-0.30}{0.0374}=2.94
\]
The sample proportion is 2.94 standard errors above the population proportion.

9.11.3 Step 3: Find the Probability
The standard normal table gives an area of 0.4984 between the mean and \(z=2.94\):
\[
P(Z>2.94)=0.50-0.4984=0.0016
\]
If the population proportion is 0.30, a random sample of 150 cases would produce a proportion of 0.41 or higher only about 0.16% of the time. The result is unusual under that assumption.

\[
z=\frac{0.41-0.30}{0.0592}=1.86
\]
The upper-tail probability is:
\[
P(Z>1.86)=0.0314
\]
The sample proportion is the same in both examples, but the larger sample provides stronger evidence that the difference is not simply chance variation.

title: 9  Sampling Distributions
text:
9.17 Looking Ahead
A sampling distribution tells us how a statistic varies across random samples. The next chapter uses that knowledge for estimation. We will use a sample statistic and its standard error to construct a range of plausible values for an unknown population parameter.

title: 9  Sampling Distributions
text:
9.18 Chapter Summary

A parameter describes a population; a statistic describes a sample.
Random samples from the same population usually produce different statistics.
A sampling distribution contains a statistic calculated from many samples of the same size.
Sampling distributions are centered at the corresponding population parameter.
Standard error describes the expected sampling variability of a statistic.
Larger samples produce smaller standard errors and more precise estimates.
Under appropriate conditions, sampling distributions are approximately normal.
A z-score locates a sample statistic in its sampling distribution.
The same statistic is more unusual when it comes from a larger random sample.
Larger samples reduce random sampling error but do not eliminate systematic bias.

title: 9  Sampling Distributions
text:
9.19 Key Terms


Central limit theorem: The principle that sampling distributions become increasingly normal under appropriate conditions as sample size grows.

Parameter: A numerical description of a population.

Population: The complete set of cases a researcher wants to understand.

Sample: A subset of cases selected from a population.

Sampling distribution: The distribution of a statistic across all possible samples of the same size.

Sampling variability: Natural differences among statistics produced by different random samples.

Standard error: The standard deviation of a sampling distribution.

Statistic: A numerical description calculated from sample data.

title: 10  Estimation and Confidence Intervals
text:
10.1 The Question
Suppose a city, Trustington, wants to know the proportion of residents who trust the police. Trustington is a really large city. Huge. Surveying every resident would be costly and time-consuming, so researchers select a random sample. The sample proportion provides a useful estimate, but another random sample would probably produce a somewhat different result.
A good estimate should therefore communicate two things: the value supported by the sample and the uncertainty surrounding it. A confidence interval combines both into a range of plausible values for a population parameter.

title: 10  Estimation and Confidence Intervals
text:
NoteCentral question



How can we use a sample to estimate an unknown population value while acknowledging uncertainty?

title: 10  Estimation and Confidence Intervals
text:
10.2 What You Will Learn
After completing this chapter, you should be able to:

Distinguish a point estimate from an interval estimate.
Explain the purpose of a confidence interval.
Calculate the estimated standard error and margin of error.
Construct 95% and 99% confidence intervals for a proportion.
Construct confidence intervals for a mean.
Interpret confidence intervals accurately.
Explain how confidence level, sample size, and variability affect interval width.

title: 10  Estimation and Confidence Intervals
text:
10.3 Point Estimates and Interval Estimates
A point estimate is a single sample statistic used to estimate a population parameter.


Population quantity
Parameter
Point estimate



Proportion
\(\pi\)
\(\hat{p}\)


Mean
\(\mu\)
\(\bar{x}\)



If 70% of sampled residents say they trust the police, then:
\[
\hat{p}=0.70
\]
The value 0.70 is the point estimate of the unknown population proportion, \(\pi\).
An interval estimate gives a range of plausible values. It acknowledges that the point estimate would vary across random samples.






ImportantAn estimate is not the parameter



The sample statistic is known because it is calculated from the data. The population parameter remains unknown. The purpose of estimation is to use the statistic to learn about that parameter.

title: 10  Estimation and Confidence Intervals
section: 10.4 The Structure of a Confidence Interval
text:
10.4 The Structure of a Confidence Interval
A confidence interval has the general form:
\[
\text{Point estimate}\pm\text{Margin of error}
\]
The margin of error combines:

a critical value, determined by the chosen confidence level; and
the standard error, which describes expected sampling variability.

\[
ME=\text{Critical value}\times SE
\]
For the confidence levels used in this chapter:


Confidence level
Critical z-value



95%
1.96


99%
2.58



Therefore:
\[
95\%\ CI=\text{Point estimate}\pm1.96(SE)
\]
\[
99\%\ CI=\text{Point estimate}\pm2.58(SE)
\]

title: 10  Estimation and Confidence Intervals
text:
10.5 Why 1.96 and 2.58?
In a standard normal distribution, approximately 95% of the area lies between \(z=-1.96\) and \(z=1.96\). Approximately 99% lies between \(z=-2.58\) and \(z=2.58\).
These critical values determine how far the interval extends on either side of the point estimate. A 99% interval uses a larger critical value and is therefore wider than a 95% interval calculated from the same sample.






NoteThe confidence–precision tradeoff



Greater confidence requires a wider interval. A wider interval is more likely to capture the parameter, but it identifies its location less precisely.

title: 10  Estimation and Confidence Intervals
text:
10.6 Confidence Interval for a Proportion
When the population proportion is unknown, its standard error is estimated using the sample proportion:
\[
\widehat{SE}_{\hat{p}}
=\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}
\]
The steps are:

Calculate the sample proportion, \(\hat{p}\).
Calculate the estimated standard error.
Multiply the standard error by the critical value.
Subtract the margin of error to obtain the lower bound.
Add the margin of error to obtain the upper bound.

title: 10  Estimation and Confidence Intervals
section: 10.7 Worked Example: Trust in the Police
text:
10.7 Worked Example: Trust in the Police
Back to Trustington where a random sample of 100 residents finds that 70% trust the police:
\[
\hat{p}=0.70,\qquad n=100
\]

10.7.1 Step 1: Calculate the Standard Error
\[
\widehat{SE}_{\hat{p}}
=\sqrt{\frac{0.70(1-0.70)}{100}}
=\sqrt{0.0021}
=0.0458
\]

10.7.2 Step 2: Calculate the 95% Margin of Error
\[
ME=1.96(0.0458)=0.0898
\]

10.7.3 Step 3: Construct the Interval
\[
0.70\pm0.0898
\]
\[
(0.6102,\ 0.7898)
\]
After rounding, the 95% confidence interval is approximately \((0.61,0.79)\).

10.7.4 Step 4: Interpret the Interval
We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.61 to 0.79 contains the true proportion of residents who trust the police.
In percentages, the plausible range is approximately 61% to 79%.

title: 10  Estimation and Confidence Intervals
text:
10.8 What Does “95% Confident” Mean?
Confidence describes the long-run performance of the method. Imagine repeatedly:

drawing a random sample of the same size;
calculating a sample proportion; and
constructing a 95% confidence interval.

Over many repetitions, approximately 95% of the intervals would contain the true population proportion. Approximately 5% would miss it.
For the one interval calculated from our data, the parameter is fixed and the interval either contains it or does not. We use the phrase “95% confident” because the method succeeds approximately 95% of the time under its assumptions.






WarningA common misinterpretation



A 95% confidence interval does not mean that 95% of residents have values inside the interval. The interval estimates a population parameter, not the distribution of individual observations.

text:
10.9 Confidence Level and Interval Width
Using the same sample, a 99% confidence interval is:
\[

\]
\[
0.70\pm0.1182=(0.5818,\ 0.8182)
\]

The 99% interval is wider because it must cover more of the sampling distribution.

title: 10  Estimation and Confidence Intervals
text:
10.11 Confidence Interval for a Mean
The same structure applies when estimating a population mean:
\[
\bar{x}\pm\text{Critical value}(\widehat{SE}_{\bar{x}})
\]
When the population standard deviation is unknown, we estimate the standard error using the sample standard deviation:
\[
\widehat{SE}_{\bar{x}}=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
This chapter uses normal critical values to establish the logic of confidence intervals. A later chapter introduces the t-distribution, which is generally used for a mean when the population standard deviation is unknown.

title: 10  Estimation and Confidence Intervals
text:
10.12 Worked Example: Respect Ratings
Eleven residents in Authoritiville rate the statement “The police department treats residents with respect” on a 1–6 scale:
\[
3,3,3,3,3,4,5,5,5,5,5
\]
For these data:
\[
n=11,\qquad \bar{x}=4.00,\qquad s=1.00
\]
The estimated standard error is:
\[
\widehat{SE}_{\bar{x}}=\frac{1.00}{\sqrt{11}}=0.3015
\]
Using the normal critical value, the 95% margin of error is:
\[
ME=1.96(0.3015)=0.5910
\]
The interval is:
\[
4.00\pm0.5910=(3.409,\ 4.591)
\]
We are 95% confident that this interval contains the population mean respect rating, subject to the assumptions of the method.

title: 10  Estimation and Confidence Intervals
text:
10.13 How Variability Affects Precision
Consider a second sample of fifteen residents in Authoritiville:
\[
2,2,2,2,2,2,2,4,6,6,6,6,6,6,6
\]
It also has a mean of 4.00, but:
\[
n=15,\qquad s=2.00
\]
Its standard error is:
\[
\widehat{SE}_{\bar{x}}=\frac{2.00}{\sqrt{15}}=0.5164
\]
Its approximate 95% interval is:
\[
4.00\pm1.96(0.5164)=(2.988,\ 5.012)
\]
Although the second sample is larger, its interval is wider because its observations are much more variable.






ImportantWhat determines precision?



Confidence intervals become narrower with a lower confidence level, a larger sample, or less variability. They become wider with a higher confidence level, a smaller sample, or more variability.

title: 10  Estimation and Confidence Intervals
text:
10.14 Assumptions and Limits
Confidence intervals quantify uncertainty produced by random sampling. Their interpretation depends on the study design and assumptions.
Before interpreting an interval, ask:

Were cases selected using a defensible sampling process?
Are observations sufficiently independent?
Was the variable measured consistently?
Is the normal approximation reasonable?
Does the population match the population named in the conclusion?

A narrow interval can be wrong when the underlying data are biased.

title: 10  Estimation and Confidence Intervals
text:
10.19 Looking Ahead
Confidence intervals begin with a sample statistic and identify plausible values for a population parameter. The next chapter approaches inference from another direction. Hypothesis testing begins with a proposed population value and asks whether the observed sample would be unusual if that proposal were true.
Both methods rely on the same foundation: sampling distributions, standard errors, and probability.

title: 10  Estimation and Confidence Intervals
text:
10.20 Chapter Summary

A point estimate is a single sample statistic used to estimate a population parameter.
A confidence interval combines a point estimate with a margin of error.
The margin of error is a critical value multiplied by the standard error.
A 95% confidence procedure captures the true parameter in approximately 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions.
Greater confidence produces a wider interval.
Larger samples generally produce narrower intervals.
Greater variability produces wider intervals for a mean.
Confidence intervals quantify random sampling uncertainty, not bias or measurement error.
Confidence intervals should be interpreted in the context of the population, sampling process, and variable.

title: 10  Estimation and Confidence Intervals
text:
10.21 Key Terms


Confidence interval: A range of plausible values for a population parameter constructed from sample data.

Confidence level: The long-run percentage of intervals produced by a method that contain the true parameter.

Critical value: The multiplier determined by the confidence level.

Interval estimate: A range used to estimate a population parameter.

Margin of error: The critical value multiplied by the standard error.

Point estimate: A single sample statistic used to estimate a population parameter.

Precision: The degree to which an estimate is narrowly specified, reflected by confidence-interval width.

title: 11  Hypothesis Testing
text:
11.1 The Question
Suppose a police department claims that officers issue an average of four traffic citations per week. A random sample from a researcher produces an average of six. The difference could mean that the department’s claim is inaccurate, or it could have arisen through ordinary sampling variability.
Hypothesis testing provides a structured way to evaluate these possibilities. We begin by assuming a specific population value, determine how unusual the sample result would be under that assumption, and then decide whether the data provide sufficient evidence against the assumption.

title: 11  Hypothesis Testing
text:
NoteCentral question



How can sample data be used to evaluate a claim about a population?

title: 11  Hypothesis Testing
text:
11.2 What You Will Learn
After completing this chapter, you should be able to:

State null and alternative hypotheses about a population mean.
Distinguish right-tailed, left-tailed, and two-tailed tests.
Explain the meaning of the significance level and p-value.
Calculate a standard error and obtained z-statistic.
Compare an obtained statistic with a critical value.
Decide whether to reject or fail to reject a null hypothesis.
Interpret a hypothesis-test result without overstating the evidence.

title: 11  Hypothesis Testing
text:
11.3 The Logic of Hypothesis Testing
A statistical hypothesis is a claim about a population parameter. Hypothesis testing compares two claims:

The null hypothesis, \(H_0\), states the value assumed for the population parameter.
The alternative hypothesis, \(H_A\), states the competing claim for which the researcher seeks evidence.

For the traffic-citation example:
\[
H_0:\mu=4
\]
\[
H_A:\mu>4
\]
The hypotheses concern the unknown population mean, \(\mu\), not the observed sample mean, \(\bar{x}\).
The test asks:

If the null hypothesis were true, how unusual would our sample result be?

If the sample result would be very unusual under \(H_0\), we reject the null hypothesis. If it would not be sufficiently unusual, we fail to reject it.






ImportantBegin by assuming the null hypothesis



A hypothesis test does not begin by assuming the researcher’s claim is true. It measures how compatible the observed sample is with the value stated by the null hypothesis.

title: 11  Hypothesis Testing
text:
11.4 Reject or Fail to Reject
A test produces one of two decisions:


Reject \(H_0\): The sample provides sufficient evidence against the null hypothesis at the selected significance level.

Fail to reject \(H_0\): The sample does not provide sufficient evidence against the null hypothesis.

Failing to reject is not the same as proving the null hypothesis true. The sample may simply be too small, too variable, or too close to the proposed value to provide strong evidence.






WarningDo not say that the null hypothesis was accepted or proved



“Fail to reject” means that the evidence was insufficient to reject the null hypothesis. It does not establish that the null hypothesis is correct.

title: 11  Hypothesis Testing
text:
11.5 Direction of the Alternative Hypothesis
The alternative hypothesis determines which part of the sampling distribution counts as evidence against \(H_0\).


Alternative hypothesis
Type of test
Evidence lies in



\(H_A:\mu>\mu_0\)
Right-tailed
Right tail


\(H_A:\mu<\mu_0\)
Left-tailed
Left tail


\(H_A:\mu\ne\mu_0\)
Two-tailed
Both tails



A directional claim must be selected before examining the result. Choosing a tail after seeing the sample would give the observed result an unfair advantage.

title: 11  Hypothesis Testing
text:
11.6 Significance Level and Critical Values
The significance level, symbolized by \(\alpha\), sets the threshold for deciding that a result is sufficiently unusual. This chapter uses:
\[
\alpha=0.05
\]
For a one-tailed test, the entire 0.05 rejection region is placed in one tail. For a two-tailed test, it is divided into 0.025 in each tail.







Test at \(\alpha=0.05\)

The area beyond the critical value is the rejection region.

title: 11  Hypothesis Testing
text:
11.7 Calculating the Test Statistic
To test a proposed population mean using the normal model:
\[
z=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\widehat{SE}_{\bar{x}}}
\]
where:


\(\bar{x}\) is the sample mean;

\(\mu_0\) is the value proposed by \(H_0\); and

\(\widehat{SE}_{\bar{x}}=s/\sqrt{n}\).

The obtained z-statistic expresses the difference between the sample mean and proposed population mean in standard-error units.
This chapter uses the normal distribution to establish the logic of testing. Chapter 12 introduces the t-distribution, which is generally used for a population mean when the population standard deviation is unknown.

title: 11  Hypothesis Testing
text:
11.8 Worked Example: Traffic Citations
A department claims that officers issue an average of four citations per week. A researcher believes the population mean is greater than four. A random sample produces:
\[
n=16,\qquad \bar{x}=6,\qquad s=4
\]

11.8.1 Step 1: State the Hypotheses
\[
H_0:\mu=4
\]
\[
H_A:\mu>4
\]
This is a right-tailed test.

11.8.2 Step 2: Calculate the Standard Error
\[
\widehat{SE}_{\bar{x}}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{16}}=1
\]

11.8.3 Step 3: Calculate the Obtained Statistic
\[
z=\frac{6-4}{1}=2.00
\]
The sample mean is two standard errors above the value proposed by \(H_0\).

11.8.4 Step 4: Make the Decision
For a right-tailed test with \(\alpha=0.05\), the critical value is 1.64:
\[
2.00>1.64
\]
We reject \(H_0\).

11.8.5 Step 5: Interpret the Result
At the 0.05 significance level, the sample provides evidence that the population mean number of citations issued per week is greater than four.

title: 11  Hypothesis Testing
text:
11.9 The p-Value
The p-value is the probability, assuming \(H_0\) is true, of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the one observed in the direction specified by \(H_A\).
For the right-tailed test with \(z=2.00\):
\[
p=P(Z\ge2.00)=0.0228
\]
Because \(p<0.05\), we reject \(H_0\). The p-value method and critical-value method reach the same decision.






WarningWhat a p-value is not



The p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. It is a probability calculated under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true.

title: 11  Hypothesis Testing
text:
11.10 One-Tailed and Two-Tailed Decisions
Suppose a department claims that the mean number of arrests per week is 80. A sample produces:
\[
n=64,\qquad \bar{x}=78.25,\qquad s=8
\]
The standard error and obtained statistic are:
\[
\widehat{SE}_{\bar{x}}=\frac{8}{\sqrt{64}}=1
\]
\[
z=\frac{78.25-80}{1}=-1.75
\]

11.10.1 Left-Tailed Claim
If the alternative is \(H_A:\mu<80\), the critical value is \(-1.64\). Because:
\[
-1.75<-1.64
\]
we reject \(H_0\). The one-tailed p-value is approximately 0.0401.

11.10.2 Two-Tailed Claim
If the alternative is \(H_A:\mu\ne80\), the critical values are \(\pm1.96\). Because:
\[
|-1.75|<1.96
\]
we fail to reject \(H_0\). The two-tailed p-value is approximately 0.0801.
The data are identical. The decision differs because the two hypotheses ask different questions and assign the rejection region differently.

title: 11  Hypothesis Testing
section: 11.11 Sample Size, Variability, and the Test Statistic
text:
11.11 Sample Size, Variability, and the Test Statistic
The obtained statistic depends on the difference from the null value and the standard error:
\[
z=\frac{\text{Observed difference}}{\text{Standard error}}
\]
A larger sample generally reduces the standard error. Greater variability increases it. Therefore, identical differences from \(\mu_0\) can produce different test statistics.
For example, another sample has:
\[
n=100,\qquad \bar{x}=78.25,\qquad s=5
\]
Then:
\[
\widehat{SE}_{\bar{x}}=\frac{5}{\sqrt{100}}=0.50
\]
\[
z=\frac{78.25-80}{0.50}=-3.50
\]
This result falls beyond both \(-1.64\) and \(-1.96\), so it rejects \(H_0\) for either the left-tailed or two-tailed alternative.






ImportantStatistical significance is not practical importance



A small p-value indicates that the result is difficult to explain through sampling variability under \(H_0\). It does not tell us whether the difference is large, important, beneficial, or harmful in practice.

title: 11  Hypothesis Testing
text:
11.12 A Complete Testing Process
Use the following sequence:

State \(H_0\) and \(H_A\) about the population parameter.
Identify whether the test is right-tailed, left-tailed, or two-tailed.
Select \(\alpha\) before examining the result.
Calculate the standard error.
Calculate the obtained test statistic.
Find the p-value or compare with the appropriate critical value.
Reject or fail to reject \(H_0\).
Interpret the result in context.
State an important limitation or what the result does not establish.

At \(\alpha=0.05\), Case 1 provides evidence that the population mean exceeds 96 minutes. Case 2 does not provide sufficient evidence that it is below 96 minutes. Under the normal-approximation procedure used here, Case 3 provides evidence that it differs from 96 minutes.
Case 3 has only four observations and an estimated population standard deviation. The normal approximation is questionable. The next chapter’s t-procedure is more appropriate and places greater weight on the uncertainty created by such a small sample.

title: 11  Hypothesis Testing
text:
11.19 Key Terms


Alternative hypothesis (\(H_A\)): The population claim for which the researcher seeks evidence.

Critical value: The boundary separating the rejection region from results that fail to reject \(H_0\).

Hypothesis testing: A procedure for evaluating a population claim using sample data.

Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): The population claim assumed when calculating the test statistic and p-value.

p-value: Assuming \(H_0\) is true, the probability of a result at least as extreme as the observed result.

Rejection region: Values of the test statistic that lead to rejection of \(H_0\).

Significance level (\(\alpha\)): The threshold used to decide whether a result is sufficiently unusual to reject \(H_0\).

Statistical significance: A result that meets the selected criterion for rejecting \(H_0\).

Test statistic: A standardized value comparing a sample result with the null hypothesis.

Two-tailed test: A test with an alternative hypothesis using \(\ne\).

One-tailed test: A test with an alternative hypothesis using \(<\) or \(>\).

title: 12  The t-Distribution
text:
12.1 The Question
The previous chapters used the normal distribution to develop the logic of confidence intervals and hypothesis testing. In practice, however, we rarely know a population’s standard deviation. We estimate it using the sample standard deviation, which introduces additional uncertainty.
The t-distribution accounts for that uncertainty. It allows us to test a claim about one population mean while recognizing that the population standard deviation must also be estimated.

title: 12  The t-Distribution
text:
NoteCentral question



How can we test a claim about one population mean when population variability is unknown?

title: 12  The t-Distribution
text:

title: 12  The t-Distribution
text:
12.3 Why Use the t-Distribution?
A z-test for a mean assumes that the population standard deviation, \(\sigma\), is known. Usually it is not. Instead, we estimate it using the sample standard deviation, \(s\):
\[
\widehat{SE}_{\bar{x}}=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
Because \(s\) varies from sample to sample, this estimate introduces uncertainty beyond ordinary sampling variability. The t-distribution accounts for that uncertainty.
Like the standard normal distribution, a t-distribution is:

symmetric around zero;
bell-shaped; and
used to calculate probabilities and critical values.

Unlike the standard normal distribution, it has heavier tails. The heavier tails require stronger evidence before rejecting a null hypothesis.







Figure 12.1: With few degrees of freedom, the t distribution has heavier tails. It approaches the standard normal distribution as degrees of freedom increase.

title: 12  The t-Distribution
text:
12.4 Degrees of Freedom
There is one standard normal distribution but many t-distributions. The appropriate shape depends on the degrees of freedom, abbreviated \(df\).
For a one-sample t-test:
\[
df=n-1
\]
Small samples have fewer degrees of freedom, heavier tails, and larger critical values. As sample size increases, the t-distribution approaches the standard normal distribution.
Appendix B, Student’s t-Distribution Critical Values, provides the critical values used in this chapter.

title: 12  The t-Distribution
text:
12.6 The One-Sample t-Test
The one-sample test statistic is:
\[
t=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}
\]
The formula resembles the z-statistic. The important change is that the decision is based on a t-distribution with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom.

title: 12  The t-Distribution
text:
12.7 Worked Example: Motion Processing Times
The Court of Reasonable Expectations claims that the mean processing time for a routine motion is 10 minutes. A defense attorney believes the true mean is greater. A random sample produces:
\[
n=9,\qquad \bar{x}=12,\qquad s=3
\]

12.7.1 Step 1: State the Hypotheses
\[
H_0:\mu=10
\]
\[
H_A:\mu>10
\]
This is a right-tailed test.

12.7.2 Step 2: Calculate the Standard Error
\[
\widehat{SE}_{\bar{x}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{9}}=1
\]

12.7.3 Step 3: Calculate the Obtained Statistic
\[
t=\frac{12-10}{1}=2.00
\]

12.7.4 Step 4: Find the Critical Value
\[
df=9-1=8
\]
For a right-tailed test with \(\alpha=0.05\) and \(df=8\):
\[
t_{critical}=1.860
\]

12.7.5 Step 5: Decide and Interpret
Because:
\[
2.00>1.860
\]
we reject \(H_0\). At the 0.05 level, the sample provides evidence that the population mean processing time exceeds 10 minutes.
If the alternative had been two-tailed, the critical value would be \(2.306\). In that case, we would fail to reject \(H_0\). As before, the direction of the alternative matters.

title: 12  The t-Distribution
text:

The t-distribution accounts for uncertainty created by estimating population variability with a sample standard deviation.

t-distribution: A family of symmetric probability distributions with tails that reflect uncertainty from estimating population variability.

t-statistic: A standardized difference expressed in estimated standard-error units.

title: 13  Comparing Two Means
text:
13.1 The Question
So far, we have been examining questions that involve one sample mean or one sample proportion with a proposed population value. Many questions in criminology and criminal justice go beyond this and compare two groups. We may want to know whether two programs have different mean outcomes, whether case processing differs across types of legal representation, or whether officers in different assignments have different mean caseloads.
An independent-samples t-test extends the same logic to the difference between two means. It compares the observed difference with the amount of variation expected from two independent samples.

title: 13  Comparing Two Means
text:
13.3 Comparing Two Population Means
Many criminal justice questions compare two groups:

Do public defender and private attorney cases have different disposition times?
Do specialist and general-assignment probation officers have different caseloads?
Do two programs produce different mean outcomes?

For two independent groups, the null hypothesis usually states that the population means are equal:
\[
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2
\]
This is equivalent to:
\[
H_0:\mu_1-\mu_2=0
\]
Possible alternatives are:
\[
H_A:\mu_1\ne\mu_2
\]
\[
H_A:\mu_1>\mu_2
\]
or:
\[
H_A:\mu_1<\mu_2
\]

title: 13  Comparing Two Means
text:
13.4 Standard Error for the Difference
Each sample contributes uncertainty. The estimated standard error of the difference is:
\[
\widehat{SE}_{\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2}
=\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}
\]
The test statistic is:
\[
t=\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-0}
{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}
\]
The zero represents the difference proposed by \(H_0\).






WarningSquare the standard deviations



The standard-error formula uses the sample variances, \(s_1^2\) and \(s_2^2\). A common mistake is to insert the standard deviations without squaring them.

13.12 Part II: What You Can Now Do
Part II began with probability and developed a sequence of ideas:

Probability describes uncertainty.
The normal distribution helps locate common and unusual outcomes.
Sampling distributions describe how statistics vary across samples.
Confidence intervals estimate unknown population parameters.
Hypothesis tests evaluate population claims.
The t-distribution supports inference about a population mean when variability is unknown.
Independent-samples t-tests evaluate differences between two population means.

These tools do not remove uncertainty. They make uncertainty visible and allow it to be incorporated into statistical reasoning.

title: 13  Comparing Two Means
text:
13.13 Chapter Summary

An independent-samples t-test evaluates a difference between two population means.
The null hypothesis usually states that the difference between population means is zero.
The standard error incorporates the sample sizes and variabilities of both groups.
The obtained t-statistic expresses the observed difference in estimated standard-error units.
This chapter uses \(n_1+n_2-2\) as a classroom degrees-of-freedom approximation.
Statistical software commonly uses Welch’s adjusted degrees of freedom.
Independent-samples tests are not appropriate for repeated or naturally paired observations.
Statistical significance does not establish practical importance or causation.

title: 13  Comparing Two Means

13.14 Key Terms

Independent samples: Samples containing different, unrelated cases.
Independent-samples t-test: A test comparing the means of two independent populations.
Mean difference: The difference between two sample or population means.
Paired observations: Measurements that are linked through repeated observations or natural matching.
Standard error of the difference: The expected sampling variability of the difference between two sample means.

B.1 Using the Table
The t distribution is used for inference about a population mean when the population standard deviation, \(\sigma\), is unknown and is estimated with the sample standard deviation, \(s\). The appropriate critical value depends on:
For a one-sample t test, \(df=n-1\). Other t tests use different degrees-of-freedom formulas.

title: Appendix B — t-Distribution Critical Values
text:
For a right-tailed test, use the positive critical value shown in the one-tailed section.
For a left-tailed test, use the negative of the listed one-tailed value.
For a two-tailed test, compare the absolute obtained statistic, \(|t|\), with the positive value in the two-tailed section.
For a confidence interval with confidence level \(1-\alpha\), use the corresponding two-tailed critical value.
If the exact degrees of freedom are not listed, use the next smaller listed value as a conservative classroom approximation.
Welch’s t test can produce noninteger degrees of freedom. Round down when using this printed table unless instructed to use software.







ImportantSelect the column before examining the result

B.2 Worked Example
Suppose a one-sample test has \(n=6\), so:
\[
df=n-1=5
\]
For a right-tailed test with \(\alpha=.05\), locate row \(df=5\) and the one-tailed \(\alpha=.05\) column. The critical value is approximately:
\[
t_{critical}=2.015
\]
Reject the null hypothesis only if the obtained t statistic is greater than 2.015. For a left-tailed test, the corresponding critical value would be \(-2.015\).







Figure B.1: Right-tail rejection region for df = 5 and alpha = .05.




The final row, \(df=\infty\), gives the corresponding standard normal critical values. As degrees of freedom increase, the t distribution approaches the standard normal distribution.

C.1 Using the Table
The chi-square distribution is used for several statistical procedures. For a chi-square test involving an \(r\times c\) contingency table, the degrees of freedom are:
\[
df=(r-1)(c-1)
\]
The table reports right-tail critical values. For a selected significance level, \(\alpha\), the area to the right of the critical value equals \(\alpha\).
Chi-square statistics cannot be negative. If the exact degrees of freedom are not listed, use the next smaller listed value as a conservative classroom approximation.

Suppose a contingency table has three rows and four columns. Its degrees of freedom are:
\[

\]
For \(df=6\) and \(\alpha=.05\), the table gives:
\[

\]
An obtained chi-square statistic greater than 12.592 falls in the right-tail rejection region. An obtained statistic at or below 12.592 does not.
